summary: Defines some common media features for describing image resolution, size, color and image representation methods that are common to web browsing, printing and fax applications.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a shared list of words for describing screens and paper, such as how sharp, how big and what colors, so devices can tell each other what they can show.

subtitle: Six named tags that let a device say how big, sharp and colorful its screen or paper is.

tldr.problem: A web server, printer driver or fax sender cannot pick the best version of a document unless the recipient can describe its own display or output capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers six media feature tags: pix-x and pix-y, dpi, ua-media, paper-size and color, each with defined value types and meanings.
tldr.outcome: A sender can pick a higher or lower resolution variant, a paper size, or a color or greyscale version to suit the recipient.

facts.label: Tags registered
facts.value: pix-x, pix-y, dpi, ua-media, paper-size, color

today: RFC 2534 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It supplies the six media feature tags for use within the registration framework of RFC 2506.

sections.title: Purpose of the Media Features
sections.content:
The work was originally motivated by web browsers needing to send their display characteristics to the web server, so the server could choose an appropriate representation. The RFC defines common media features by which a recipient informs a sender about how it handles messages, using the registration form of RFC 2506.

Variants would typically be higher or lower resolution images. For a printer, the result is higher quality output. For a small screen device such as a cellphone or portable digital assistant, the result is faster transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: If a tiny phone and a big printer both ask for a picture, each should get the version that suits it. To do that, they first have to say what they can handle.

sections.title: Size and Resolution Tags
sections.content:
The pix-x and pix-y tags give the horizontal and vertical display size of the recipient in pixels, for display or print. Their value type is a signed integer. The RFC's example is that a web application for a 240x480 display might use different HTML pages than one for a 1024x768 display.

The dpi tag gives the resolution the recipient can display or print without loss, in pixels per inch. Its value type is rational, so SI-based devices fit: dpi=19558/100 represents 77 dots per centimeter. Printing and fax applications typically choose a representation by resolution rather than pixel size. The tag only covers uniform resolution, even though some devices have non-square pixels.
sections.plainLanguage: One tag tells how many dots wide and tall the screen is. Another tells how finely packed the dots are.

sections.title: Device Media and Paper Size
sections.content:
The ua-media tag says what kind of media the recipient's device uses. It is a token with an equality relationship. Values include screen (a refreshable display), screen-paged (a display that cannot scroll), stationery (separately cut opaque sheets), transparency, envelope, envelope-plain and continuous (continuously connected opaque sheets). A typical use is choosing between a rendition meant to be printed and one meant to be displayed.

The paper-size tag is also a token with an equality relationship. Typical values are letter (8.5x11.0 inches), a4 (210x297 mm), b4 (250x353 mm), a3 (297x420 mm) and legal (8.5x14 inches). The RFC notes that absolute resolution and pixel sizes are more precise and predictable, but some applications find paper size useful in addition. Not all of the paper may have a printable area.
sections.plainLanguage: One tag says whether the output is a screen, a sheet of paper or an envelope. Another names the paper size, like A4 or letter.

sections.title: The Color Tag
sections.content:
The color tag indicates a gross level of capability to handle color, chosen from a limited set of tokens with an equality relationship. The values are binary (black-and-white or other bi-level), grey (more than two levels of intensity), limited (a small number of colors, at most a few under 32), mapped (colors mapped to a multi-component color space, enough levels to show a continuous tone photograph but in a more limited space) and full (full continuous tone color).

The RFC suggests that web applications may choose between color, grey or binary representations, and gives the example of someone preparing different restaurant direction maps for each kind of value. The intended usage is listed as COMMON.
sections.plainLanguage: This tag says how many colors something can show, from only black and white all the way up to a full-color photo.

sections.title: Examples of Use
sections.content:
The RFC gives illustrative examples. The syntax for combining features is purely illustrative and not normative.

  • pix-x<=1024, pix-y<=768 might be used for a 1024x768 display.
  • dpi=300 might be used for a 300 dpi printer.
  • paper-size=a4 indicates the display size is 210x297mm.
sections.plainLanguage: You write short notes like 'dpi=300' to say 'my printer is this sharp'.

sections.title: Registration
sections.content: The document calls for registering the feature tags pix-x, pix-y, dpi, ua-media, paper-size and color as per RFC 2506. Each registration lists an ASN.1 identifier; the identifiers appear as 1.3.6.1.8.1.1 through 1.3.6.1.8.1.6, and the IANA section says they should be assigned and replaced in the body of the registration.
sections.plainLanguage: The tags go into an official list so everybody uses the same names.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The only concern the RFC raises is that wrong media feature information attributed to a recipient might cause a sender to send content the recipient cannot actually process, which would cause a denial of service.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone lies about what a device can show, it may be sent something it cannot use.

items.label: Greyscale
items.desc: More than two levels of intensity.

items.label: Few colors
items.desc: A small number of colors, such as a highlight printer or pen plotter.

items.label: Mapped color
items.desc: Pixel values mapped to a multi-component color space.
